Introduction

Starting a Child Care Facility in Nevada represents a meaningful opportunity to serve infants, toddlers, preschool, and school-age children while building a compliant, sustainable care business. Oversight and funding are administered by the Nevada Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), Division of Welfare and Supportive Services (DWSS), which manages both licensing and key financial support programs. Reimbursement and program funding are coordinated through the state’s Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) subsidy program, which has a significant annual budget.

With strong demand and capacity gaps, especially in rural counties, and reimbursement rates of approximately $58 per day for subsidized infant/toddler care, Nevada offers a market with significant regional opportunities for providers prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements. The state’s growing communities and workforce needs create a stable foundation for child care services, particularly for those offering specialized programs or flexible scheduling.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Child Care Facility in Nevada, from understanding state regulations and licensing with the DWSS to staffing your center, managing reimbursement, and preparing for inspections. Whether you are opening a small family home or a large commercial center, this framework will help you build a business that is both impactful and successful.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Nevada’s Child Care Facility Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Nevada’s Child Care Facility Regulations

Nevada regulates Child Care Facilities through the Nevada Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), Division of Welfare and Supportive Services (DWSS). This agency is responsible for overseeing the licensure, regulation, and ongoing compliance of all child care facilities to ensure the health, safety, and well-being of children. The primary regulations are outlined in the Nevada Administrative Code (NAC), specifically ARM Title 37 Chapter 101. Providers serving Medicaid or federally funded populations, such as those utilizing the 1915(c) HCBS waiver (NV.0211.R06.01) for children with high needs, must also comply with federal frameworks from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF).

The regulatory framework emphasizes child safety, adequate supervision through mandated staff-to-child ratios, and staff qualifications. Key compliance areas include maintaining a safe physical environment, ensuring all staff have passed background checks, documenting daily activities, and adhering to strict health and sanitation protocols. Licenses in Nevada typically require renewal every one year, contingent upon a successful annual inspection and continued compliance with all state regulations.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Before you begin the licensing process, you must decide on the specific model for your child care business. Nevada supports multiple program types, each with different licensing, staffing, and physical plant requirements. Your choice will impact your startup costs, revenue potential, and the population you serve.

Nevada supports multiple Child Care Facility variants, each with different licensing, staffing, and reimbursement requirements:

  • Child Care Center: A commercial, non-residential facility designed to care for larger groups of children, typically segregated by age (infants, toddlers, preschoolers). These have the most stringent facility and staffing requirements but also the highest revenue potential.
  • Family/Group Child Care Home: A smaller program operated out of a provider’s residence. Family homes have a smaller capacity, while group homes can serve more children, often with the help of an additional staff member. These offer a lower-cost entry point into the market.
  • Infant/Toddler Specialty Care: Programs focusing exclusively on the high-demand niche for children under three years old. This model capitalizes on the higher subsidy rates and long waitlists for infant care but requires adherence to the strictest staff-to-child ratios (1:4).
  • Specialized Needs Programs: Facilities equipped to serve children with high needs, developmental disabilities, or medical complexities. These programs can leverage specialized funding through the 1915(c) HCBS waiver and require staff with advanced training.

Program size typically ranges from small family homes serving 6-12 children to large centers with capacity for over 100 children. Demand is strongest in rural counties, where there are fewer facilities and documented longer waitlists. Urban and suburban areas of Clark and Washoe counties also have consistent demand, but competition is higher. Regions like Elko, Nye, and Humboldt counties may offer significant entry opportunities with less competition for well-prepared providers.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Establishing the correct legal and business foundation is a critical early step. Providers in Nevada typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC), S-Corporation, or Non-Profit Corporation. Each structure has different implications for liability, taxation, and governance, so consulting with a legal and financial professional is highly recommended.

To become a licensed provider, you must complete several key administrative steps:

  • Register your business entity with the Nevada Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS, which is necessary for hiring staff.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability and professional liability insurance. Workers’ compensation insurance is mandatory once you hire employees.
  • Submit a comprehensive licensing application to the DHHS Division of Welfare and Supportive Services (DWSS). This packet includes your business information, facility plans, background check authorizations for all principals, and draft policies and procedures.

Licensing timelines in Nevada generally range from 6 to 12 months. This timeframe depends heavily on the completeness of your application, the time it takes to complete facility renovations and pass a fire marshal inspection, the processing of background checks, and the scheduling of the final on-site licensing survey by the DWSS.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is essential for securing funding and guiding your operational strategy. It should include detailed financial projections based on Nevada-specific data.

Startup costs in Nevada typically range from $50,000 to $250,000+, depending on the facility type, size, and location. Major expenses include building lease deposits, renovations to meet code, purchasing furniture and age-appropriate equipment, licensing fees, insurance premiums, and initial payroll.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by staffing, which represents 50-60% of total costs due to the state’s mandated staff-to-child ratios. Other significant costs include rent or mortgage, utilities, insurance, food, and classroom supplies.

Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges in Nevada include:

  • CCDF Subsidy (Infant/Toddler): Approximately $58 per child, per day.
  • Private Pay (Infant/Toddler): Often ranges from $65-$85 per day, particularly in urban areas.
  • Private Pay (Preschool): Typically ranges from $50-$70 per day.
  • HCBS Waiver Services: Specialized, higher rates may be available for providing care to children with documented high needs.

Providers operating at a target occupancy of 85% or higher generally achieve 5% to 15% profit margins. The extended break-even timeline noted in market research underscores the importance of careful financial management, controlling costs, and maximizing enrollment from day one.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Your physical location must meet strict state regulations to ensure the safety and well-being of children. Finding a compliant property is one of the most challenging aspects of opening a child care facility.

Key facility requirements in Nevada include:

  • Minimum square footage per child for indoor activity space (typically 35 sq. ft.) and outdoor play areas (typically 75 sq. ft.).
  • Adequate, child-safe restrooms and multiple handwashing stations accessible to children.
  • A designated, safe outdoor play space that is enclosed by a fence of a specified height and free of hazards.
  • A kitchen or food preparation area that meets local health department codes for sanitation and food safety.
  • Full compliance with local and state fire safety codes, including functional smoke detectors, fire extinguishers, clearly marked exits, and approved evacuation plans.

When selecting a location, you must consider local zoning laws first—many commercial properties are not automatically zoned for child care. Other important factors include accessibility for parents, proximity to elementary schools and large employers, and the availability of a qualified workforce in the area.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your staff is the heart of your program and the primary driver of quality and compliance. Nevada’s regulations set specific qualification and training requirements for all personnel, as well as strict staff-to-child ratios that must be maintained at all times.

Required roles typically include:

  • Director: The lead administrator who must meet specific educational (e.g., a degree in Early Childhood Education) and experience qualifications set by the DWSS.
  • Lead Teachers: Responsible for a specific classroom or age group, these individuals must have credentials or experience relevant to the children they teach (infant, toddler, or preschool).
  • Assistant Teachers/Aides: Support lead teachers in supervision, activities, and care routines to help maintain required ratios.
  • Support Staff: Depending on the size of your center, you may also need a cook, administrative assistant, or janitorial staff.

Nevada’s staff-to-child ratios are critical for licensing:

  • Infants (0-12 months): 1 staff member for every 4 infants (1:4)
  • Toddlers (1-2 years): 1 staff member for every 6 toddlers (1:6)
  • Preschool (3-5 years): 1 staff member for every 10 children (1:10)
  • School-age (6+ years): 1 staff member for every 20 children (1:20)

All staff must complete mandatory training, including First Aid and CPR certification, recognition and reporting of child abuse and neglect, and initial orientation on facility policies. The state also mandates a specific number of ongoing annual continuing education hours in child development, health, and safety to ensure staff remain current on best practices.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Comprehensive, written policies and procedures are the backbone of a compliant child care operation. The DWSS requires a detailed policy manual to be submitted with your license application and available on-site for inspection at all times. These documents guide your staff, inform parents, and demonstrate your commitment to regulatory standards.

Nevada requires written policies covering key operational areas, including:

  • Health and safety procedures (including illness exclusion, emergency evacuation plans, and accident protocols).
  • Guidance and discipline policies that promote positive behavior and prohibit corporal punishment.
  • Daily schedules and curriculum plans that outline age-appropriate activities.
  • Staffing and supervision plans that detail how ratios will be maintained throughout the day, including during naps and outdoor play.
  • Enrollment, admission, and disenrollment policies that are communicated clearly to families.
  • Medication administration protocols, including documentation and parental consent.
  • Transportation plans (if applicable).

In addition to facility-wide policies, individual care or service plans must be developed for each child, especially those with allergies, medical conditions, or special needs. These plans must be developed in partnership with parents, reviewed regularly, and documented meticulously per Nevada and federal rules.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Once you are on the path to licensure, you need a strategy to fill your classrooms. Unlike some businesses, traditional advertising is often less effective for child care than building a strong network of professional referrals.

In Nevada, referrals for child care facilities typically come from:

  • Nevada’s Child Care Resource and Referral (CCR&R) network: This state-supported agency helps parents find licensed care. Getting your facility listed is a crucial first step.
  • Local school districts and early intervention programs: These organizations often need to refer families who require child care or specialized services.
  • Corporate partnerships: Developing relationships with large local employers to offer workforce-aligned care can create a stable enrollment pipeline.
  • Online directories and parent word-of-mouth: A professional website with clear information and positive online reviews is essential.
  • Pediatricians and family health clinics: Medical professionals are a trusted source of referrals for new parents seeking quality care.

Successful providers focus on building a reputation for high-quality care, excellent communication, and unwavering compliance. Your best marketing tool is a safe, happy, and well-run facility that generates positive word-of-mouth from satisfied families.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Receiving your license is the beginning, not the end, of your compliance journey. Ongoing oversight in Nevada is conducted by inspectors from the DHHS Division of Welfare and Supportive Services (DWSS). These surveyors will conduct unannounced annual inspections and may also visit in response to any complaints.

Inspections are comprehensive and focus on verifying compliance with all aspects of the Nevada Administrative Code. Common deficiencies cited during surveys often include:

  • Failure to maintain required staff-to-child ratios, especially during staff breaks or transitions.
  • Incomplete staff files, such as missing background checks, training certificates, or health records.
  • Hazards in the physical environment, such as unsecured cleaning supplies, broken playground equipment, or tripping hazards.
  • Improper documentation of attendance, meals served, or incident reports.

To ensure you are always ready for an inspection, implement a system of continuous quality improvement. This includes conducting regular self-audits, maintaining organized and up-to-date records in an “audit-ready” format, and providing ongoing staff training. Proactive compliance is far less stressful and more effective than reacting to a list of deficiencies from a state surveyor.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to open a Child Care Facility in Nevada?

Opening a child care facility in Nevada typically takes 6 to 12 months. This includes business planning, securing a location, completing renovations, the licensing application process with DWSS, and passing all required inspections.

What licenses are required?

You need a Child Care Facility license from the Nevada Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), Division of Welfare and Supportive Services (DWSS). The specific type of license depends on whether you are opening a center, a group home, or a family home.

What reimbursement is available?

Reimbursement is available through Nevada’s Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) subsidy program, administered by DWSS. Rates are approximately $58 per day for infants/toddlers. Additional funding may be available for serving children with high needs through the 1915(c) HCBS waiver.

Conclusion

Starting a Child Care Facility in Nevada is a complex but rewarding venture that addresses a critical need within the community. Success requires careful planning to navigate the financial hurdles, a deep understanding of the regulatory landscape managed by the DWSS, and a steadfast commitment to operational discipline. Providers who invest in compliance, hire and train qualified staff, and build strong referral relationships are positioned for long-term success and a positive impact on the lives of children and families across the state.
